title: Accumulating a rate
objectives: Recover a total amount from its rate of change.
Read a running total, its peaks and its net change from the graph of a rate.

screens.prose: Cash flows into a fund at a steady rate through each day, but the rate changes from day to day. Each bar shows one day's rate, in £ thousand per day.
screens.question: How much cash came in over the five days, in £ thousand?

widget.label: Cash in over the week, £ thousand

hints.text: How much cash arrives on Monday alone?
Monday's rate is £120k per day, for one day: £120k.
Do the same for each day and add.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each day adds its rate times one day. Add the five days.

byKey.average: You averaged the rates: £100k per day is the typical day. The week's total is five days of that.
byKey.peak: That is Wednesday, the busiest day. Add every day's cash.
byKey.one-day: That is Monday alone. Add every day's cash.

explain.text: Each bar is one day wide, so its area, rate times 1 day, is that day's cash. The week's total, £500k, is the total area of the bars. A rate times a time is an amount.

canvas.caption: Total area of the bars: 500, so £500k

screens.prose: A new fund's inflows ramp up: $t$ days after launch the rate is $r(t) = 20t$ £ thousand per day. The shaded area up to day $T$ is the cash in so far. Slide $T$.
screens.question: When has half of the £360k arrived? Give $T$ to two decimal places.

widget.accept: Any value from 4.18 to 4.30. Exactly $\sqrt{18} \approx 4.243$ days.
widget.label: Day T

hints.text: Half of £360k is £180k. Watch the caption.
At day 4 the caption shows £160k. Go a little further.
The caption passes £180k between day 4.20 and day 4.25.

feedback.correct: Half has arrived at about day 4.24.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the caption reads about £180k.

byKey.half-time: At day 3, halfway in time, only £90k has arrived: a quarter. The rate is low early on.
byKey.end: By day 6 all £360k has arrived. Half arrives earlier.

explain.text: Half, £180k, has arrived when the triangle's area $\tfrac12 \cdot T \cdot 20T = 10T^2$ reaches 180: $T = \sqrt{18} \approx 4.24$ days. Halfway in time, only a quarter has arrived. The slow early days add little area.

screens.prose: The cash in by day $T$ is the area under the rate from 0 to $T$, written $$A(T) = \int_0^T r(t)\,dt$$ This is the **accumulated amount**. Here $r(t) = 20t$.
screens.question: What is $A(5)$, in £ thousand?

hints.text: The shaded region is a triangle.
Its base is 5 days and its height is $r(5) = 100$.
$\tfrac12 \times 5 \times 100 = 250$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the area of the shaded triangle.

byKey.rate: 100 is the rate at day 5, in £k per day. The amount is the area under the rate.
byKey.box: $100 \times 5$ assumes the rate was £100k a day all along. It started at 0, so the region is a triangle.
byKey.half-rate: That is half the final rate. Multiply by the 5 days as well.

explain.text: The region is a triangle with base 5 and height 100, so $A(5) = 250$: £250k. The rate at day 5 is only one height on the graph. The amount is the whole area behind it.

screens.prose: A van pulls away, speeding up steadily to 20 metres per second over 10 seconds, then holds that speed. Speed is the rate at which distance builds up.
screens.question: How far does the van travel in the first 30 seconds?

hints.text: Split the region at $t = 10$.
A triangle from 0 to 10, then a rectangle from 10 to 30.
$\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 20 + 20 \times 20$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the triangle up to 10 seconds and the rectangle after it.

byKey.top-speed: $20 \times 30$ assumes top speed from the start. In the first 10 seconds the van was slower.
byKey.triangle: That treats the whole region as one triangle. After 10 seconds the speed stays at 20.
byKey.cruise: That is the steady part alone. Add the 100 m covered while speeding up.

explain.text: Speeding up: a triangle of $\tfrac12 \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ m. Cruising: a rectangle of $20 \times 20 = 400$ m. Distance is the area under speed: 500 m.

screens.prose: A trading position earns at a rate of $p(t) = 400 - 200t$ pounds per hour. After two hours the rate turns negative: the position starts losing money.
screens.question: What is the position's P&L after 3 hours?

hints.text: Gains add; losses subtract.
The gain from 0 to 2 is a triangle of $\tfrac12 \times 2 \times 400$. The loss from 2 to 3 is $\tfrac12 \times 1 \times 200$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the signed area from 0 to 3.

byKey.stop: £400 is the P&L at hour 2. From then on the rate is negative and P&L drains away.
byKey.area: That adds the loss as if it were a gain. The region below the axis counts negative.
byKey.rate: That is the rate at hour 3, in £ per hour. The P&L is the signed area up to hour 3.

explain.text: The gain to hour 2 is $\tfrac12 \times 2 \times 400 = \text{£}400$. The loss from hour 2 to 3 is $\tfrac12 \times 1 \times 200 = \text{£}100$. So the P&L is the signed area, £300.

screens.prose: The same position over 4 hours, with P&L rate $p(t) = 400 - 200t$ pounds per hour.
screens.question: When during the 4 hours is the running P&L highest?

options.text: At $t = 0$, where the rate is highest
options.why: You read the rate as the P&L. At $t = 0$ the rate is highest, but nothing has been earned yet: the P&L is 0.

options.text: At $t = 2$, where the rate is zero

options.why: From hour 2 the rate is negative, so the P&L falls. By hour 4 it is back to 0.
At hour 1 the rate is still positive, so the P&L is still rising.

hints.text: While the rate is positive, is the P&L rising or falling?
The rate is positive before hour 2 and negative after it.
The P&L stops rising exactly where the rate stops being positive.

feedback.correct: The P&L peaks where the rate crosses zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The P&L rises while the rate is positive and falls while it is negative.

byKey.start: You read the rate as the P&L. A high rate means the P&L is rising fast, not that it is large. At $t = 0$ it is still 0.

explain.text: The P&L rises while the rate is positive and falls once it turns negative. So it peaks at hour 2, at £400, then gives it all back by hour 4. The total is largest where the rate is zero, not where the rate is largest.

screens.prose: Every time, the total change was the signed area under the rate: $$\text{change from } a \text{ to } b = \int_a^b r(t)\,dt$$ The running total $A(T) = \int_0^T r(t)\,dt$ climbs where $r > 0$ and falls where $r < 0$. How steeply it climbs at $T$ is set by $r(T)$; the next level makes this exact.
screens.question: When is the running total $A$ climbing fastest?

options.why: The largest total comes where the rate is zero, as with the P&L. There $A$ is flat, not climbing.
There $A$ stops climbing: it is at a peak or a dip.

options.text: Never: a total grows at a constant speed
options.why: Only a constant rate gives constant growth. The fund's cash came in faster and faster as $r$ grew.

hints.text: Think of the fund: when did the cash pile up fastest?
Each day adds about $r(T)$ times one day, so the biggest rate adds the most.

feedback.correct: The bigger the rate, the faster the total climbs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how much $A$ grows over one short step $\Delta t$.

explain.text: Over a short step $\Delta t$, the total grows by about $r(T)\,\Delta t$. So it climbs fastest where the rate is largest, and is flat where the rate is zero. The slope of the running total is the rate.

screens.prose: Why is the total change exactly $\int_a^b r(t)\,dt$, when the rate keeps changing? Build the argument.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Cut $[a, b]$ into $n$ pieces of length $\Delta t = \tfrac{b - a}{n}$; the total change sums the pieces' changes
Each piece's rate lies between its lowest and highest values, so its change lies between those rates times $\Delta t$
Adding over the pieces, the total change lies between a lower and an upper Riemann sum of $r$
Both sums tend to $\int_a^b r(t)\,dt$ as $n \to \infty$, so the total change is squeezed to equal it

hints.text: Start by cutting the time into pieces.
Bound each piece before adding the pieces up.
Cut, bound each piece, add the bounds, then let $n$ grow.

feedback.correct: Each line builds on the one above.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The limit can only come once the change is trapped between two sums.

byKey.f4: Letting $n$ grow comes last, once the change sits between two sums.
byKey.f3: The pieces must be bounded one at a time before their bounds are added.

explain.text: Each piece's change is trapped between its lowest and highest rate times $\Delta t$. Added up, the total change sits between two Riemann sums. Both converge to the integral, so the change equals it: the same squeeze as last lesson.

screens.prose: A £10m floating-rate note pays interest at a rate reset with the market. Its coupon rate is 4% a year for 30 days, then 4.5% a year for 60 days. Interest accrues daily on an actual/365 basis: £1,095.89 a day, then £1,232.88 a day.
screens.question: How much interest has accrued after the 90 days?

hints.text: Each piece of the rate is a rectangle: rate times days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each rectangle's area, rate times days, and add.

byKey.average: You averaged 4% and 4.5% as if each ran 45 days. The higher rate ran twice as long.
byKey.first-rate: That keeps 4% for all 90 days. The rate reset to 4.5% after day 30.
byKey.second-rate: That uses 4.5% for all 90 days. The first 30 days accrued at 4%.

explain.text: The two rectangles hold $30 \times 1{,}095.89 = \text{£}32{,}876.71$ and $60 \times 1{,}232.88 = \text{£}73{,}972.60$: about £106,849 in all. A bond's accrued interest is the area under its accrual rate. When the rate moves every day, the integral does the adding.

ideas: A rate times a time is an amount, so the area under a rate is the total it builds up.
Parts of the rate below the axis take away: the net change is the signed area.
The running total climbs fastest where the rate is largest and peaks where the rate crosses zero.

formula.name: Total change from a rate
formula.note: Distance from speed, P&L from a P&L rate, volume from a volume rate, accrued interest from a coupon rate.

summary.trap: A large rate is not a large total. The P&L peaks where its rate is zero, not where the rate is highest.

quiz.prose: Shares trade at 2,000 a minute for the first 15 minutes after the open. Then they trade at 500 a minute for the next 30 minutes.
quiz.question: How many shares trade in those 45 minutes?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each rate by its own number of minutes, then add.

byKey.rates: You added the two rates. Each rate runs for its own number of minutes.
byKey.average: You averaged the rates over all 45 minutes. The slow rate ran twice as long.
byKey.first: That is the first 15 minutes. Add the 15,000 traded afterwards.

explain.text: $2{,}000 \times 15 = 30{,}000$ and $500 \times 30 = 15{,}000$. Total volume is the area under the volume rate: 45,000 shares.

quiz.prose: A car starts from rest with speed $v(t) = 3t$ metres per second.
quiz.question: How far does it travel in the first 4 seconds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the area under the speed from 0 to 4.

byKey.final: 12 is the speed at 4 seconds, in metres per second. Distance is the area under the speed.
byKey.box: $12 \times 4$ assumes top speed from the start. The car started at rest, so the region is a triangle.

explain.text: Speed rises from 0 to 12 over 4 seconds, so the area is a triangle: $\tfrac12 \times 4 \times 12 = 24$ m.

quiz.prose: A strategy loses at a steady £50 an hour for 6 hours, then gains £80 an hour for 2 hours.
quiz.question: What is its P&L over the 8 hours?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Losses count negative: find the signed area.

byKey.area: That adds the losses as gains. The £300 lost counts against the £160 gained.
byKey.rates: You added the two rates. Multiply each by its hours first.
byKey.gain: That is the gain alone. The first 6 hours lost £300.

explain.text: The loss is a rectangle below the axis, $-50 \times 6 = -300$. The gain is $80 \times 2 = 160$. The signed area, $-140$, is the P&L: still a loss.

quiz.prose: A £1,000,000 bond pays a fixed coupon of 6% a year. Interest accrues daily on an actual/365 basis.
quiz.question: How much interest accrues over 73 days?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The accrual rate is £60,000 a year; multiply by the fraction of a year.

byKey.year: That is a full year's coupon. Only 73 of 365 days have passed.
byKey.days: You multiplied by 73 days without dividing the annual rate by 365.
byKey.daily: That is one day's interest. Multiply by the 73 days.

explain.text: The accrual rate is $\tfrac{60{,}000}{365} \approx \text{£}164.38$ a day, constant. Over 73 days the rectangle's area is $60{,}000 \times \tfrac{73}{365} = \text{£}12{,}000$, a fifth of the coupon.
